Xylose and Arabinose are both aldopentoses (five-carbon sugars with an aldehyde group). They differ at two stereocentres: typically C-2 and C-3. Since diastereomers differ at one or more (but not all) chiral centres and are not mirror images, xylose and arabinose qualify as diastereoisomers, not epimers.

**Optical Isomerism (Option A):** Two molecules with same molecular formula, but differ in the way they turn the plain polarised lights. The orientation of the —H an —OH groups around the carbon atom adjacent to the terminal alcohol carbon (carbon 5 in glucose) etermines whether the sugar beongs to the d or l series. The isomer that turns the light to the right side is called dextrorotatory (d/ +) The isomer that turns the light to the right side is called Levorotatory (l / -)
**Enantiomerism (Option C):** Exact mirror image of the carbon atoms. Another name for enantiomerism is Racemism.
**Epimerism (Option D):** Epimers differ at only one chiral centre. Since xylose and arabinose differ at two chiral centres, they are not epimers.
**Stereoisomerism:** A broad category of isomerism where molecules have the same molecular formula and connectivity of atoms but differ in the spatial arrangement of their atoms.
**Optical Isomerism (Option A):** Here the two molecules have the same molecular formula, but they differ in the way they turn the plane polarized light.
The orientation of the —H and —OH groups around the carbon atom adjacent to the termina alcohol carbon (carbon 5 in glucose) determines whether the sugar belongs to the d or l series.
The isomer that turns the light to the right side is called Dextrorotatory (d/ +) The isomer that turns the light to the left side is called Levorotatory (l / -)
Example: Lactic acid, which exists as two enantiomers: L-lactic acid and D-lactic acid.
**Functional Isomerism (Option B):** Two molecules have the same molecular formula but different functional groups.
Example: Ethanol (an alcohol) and dimethyl ether (an ether) both have the formula C2H6O but different functional groups and properties.

Flow cytometry is used to detect the absence or reduced expression of surface proteins CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells. These proteins are typically absent or deficient in PNH due to the genetic mutation affecting their GPI anchors.
**Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH):** A rare, acquired blood disorder characterized by the destruction of red blood cells due to a genetic mutation affecting cell membrane protection.
**Cause:** Mutation in the PIGA gene. Defective synthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors, which are crucial for attaching protective proteins to red blood cells.
**Key Proteins Involved:**

items.text: **CD55 (Decay Accelerating Factor):** Prevents complement system activation on the red blood cell surface.
**CD59 (Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis)** inhibits the formation of the complement system's membrane attack complex.
**Bone Marrow Biopsy(Option A):** This test is used to diagnose various bone marrow disorders but is not specific for PNH.
**Serum Ferritin Test(Option C):** This test measures iron storage levels and is not specific to PNH. It is more useful for diagnosing iron-related disorders.

**Haemoglobin Electrophoresis(Option D):** This test separates different types of haemoglobin but does not diagnose PNH. It is used to diagnose hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease or thalassemia.

blocks.text: Hunter syndrome arises due to a lack of the enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase and follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. In contrast, Hurler syndrome is due to a deficiency in the enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner (Option B).

**Both disorders result in the buildup of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate in tissues (Option C):** However, corneal clouding, which is observed in Hurler syndrome, is not typically seen in Hunter syndrome (Option A).

blocks.text: Hyaluronic acid is predominantly found in connective tissues, tendons, synovial fluid, and the vitreous humor of the eye. It serves as a crucial lubricant in joint cavities, helping to maintain joint health and mobility. A deficiency in hyaluronic acid can lead to joint pain and reduced mobility due to insufficient lubrication in the synovial fluid.

blocks.title: Functions of Various Mucopolysaccharides
rows: Serves as a lubricant in joint cavities and contributes to the structure of connective tissues
Acts as an anticoagulant by activating antithrombin III, which inactivates thrombin and other clotting factors
Provides structural support to connective tissues and contributes to their resilience and elasticity
Contributes to the structure of the skin, blood vessels, and heart valves

blocks.text: Dermatan sulfate contributes to the structure of the skin, blood vessels, and heart valves. A deficiency or dysfunction in dermatan sulfate can lead to issues with the structural integrity of the skin and blood vessels, resulting in symptoms such as hyperextensible skin and increased vascular fragility.

blocks.title: Locations of Various Mucopolysaccharides
rows: Connective tissues, tendons, synovial fluid, vitreous humor

blocks.text: The image depicts Keratan sulfate, identifiable by its unique composition of galactose and N-acetylglucosamine, along with possible sulfate groups. It is unique among glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) because it lacks uronic acid. It is primarily found in the cornea and cartilage, contributing to their structural properties.
**Identification Tips:** Look for the presence of galactose as one of the primary sugars in the disaccharide unit.
N-acetylglucosamine can be identified by the presence of the N-acetyl group (CH₃CONH). Sulfate groups may be attached to either of the sugar moieties, contributing to the molecule's negative charge.

blocks.text: The diagnosis here points to lactose intolerance, a digestion defect caused by the enzyme lactase deficiency. It presents with symptoms like osmotic diarrhoea, flatulence, bloating, and frothy stools. The investigation of choice for lactose intolerance is the Hydrogen breath test and methane breath test.
Other tests include:

items.text: **Stool acidity test:** Unabsorbed lactose is fermented by colonic bacteria into lactic acid, lowering stool pH.
**Dietary elimination:** Elimination of certain foods reduces the symptoms.
**Milk tolerance test:** 500ml milk to be consumed and to note the blood glucose level to see malabsorption
**Lactose tolerance test:** Checks lactose absorption after consuming a lactose-containing liquid.
**Small intestine biopsy:** Done to find secondary causes only.

blocks.text: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) is the rate-limiting enzyme in galactose metabolism.
**Galactose Metabolism:**

items.text: **Dietary Source** Lactose in milk and milk products.
**Structure** Aldohexose and it is the 4th epimer of glucose.
**Metabolism Site** Metabolized exclusively by the liver. Therefore, galactose tolerance tests can assess liver function.

blocks.text: **Galactose Metabolism:**

items.text: **1) Phosphorylation** Galactose is phosphorylated by galactokinase to form galactose-1-phosphate. (Option A ruled out) ATP is the phosphate donor.

**2) Uridine diphosphate-galactose (UDP-galactose) formation** Galactose-1-phosphate converts to UDP-galactose and glucose-1-phosphate via an exchange reaction with UDP-glucose The reaction is catalyzed by Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT: rate-limiting enzyme in galactose metabolism) (Option B ruled out)

**3) UDP-galactose conversion to UDP-glucose** UDP-galactose is isomerized to UDP-glucose by UDP-hexose-4-epimerase. (Option C ruled out) The new UDP-glucose can enter biosynthetic reactions (e.g., glycogenesis) and the GALT reaction.
**4) UDP-galactose in biosynthetic reactions** UDP-galactose serves as an active donor of galactose for synthesizing lactose, glycoproteins, glycolipids and glycosaminoglycans.

blocks.text: If dietary galactose is unavailable, UDP-galactose can be synthesized from UDP-glucose via UDP-hexose-4-epimerase.
**Aldolase reductase (Option D):** reduces galactose to galactitol and glucose to sorbitol. It is not the rate-limiting of galactose metabolism
Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) deficiency is seen in classic g alactosemia, in which galactose-1-phosphate and, therefore, galactose accumulate.
Galactose-1-phosphate Uridyl transferase (GALT) Deficiency
Severely deficient in individuals with Classic Galactosemia in which galactose-1-phosphate and, therefore, galactose accumulate. (Option B) It Is an inborn error of metabolism
Accumulation
Accumulated galactose is shunted into side pathways like galactitol production. Aldose reductase catalyzes it.
Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the liver, inhibiting galactokinase and glycogen phosphorylase, leading to hypoglycemia.

items.text: **Bilirubin** Reduced bilirubin uptake and conjugation, increasing unconjugated bilirubin in blood
**Symptoms**
Hypoglycemia, hypophosphatemia, hyperuricemia, lactic acidosis
Hepatomegaly, jaundice, Severe mental retardation
Galactosuria (galactose excreted in urine)
Cataracts due to dulcitol accumulation in the lens
Tubular damage and generalized aminoaciduria
**Diagnosis**
Clinical manifestations (e.g., congenital cataract), presence of galactose in urine and elevated blood galactose levels
Prenatal diagnosis via amniocentesis
Detection of heterozygous parents by elevated galactose levels after a galactose load
**Complications in untreated cases**
E. coli sepsis, Fanconi syndrome
Feeding problems, Failure to thrive, Hepatocellular damage, Bleeding
**Treatment** Withdrawal of galactose and lactose from the diet.

blocks.text: **GALT deficiency is a part of the newborn screening panel**
**Galactokinase (Option A):** phosphorylate galactose to form galactose 1-phosphate. Its deficiency leads to less severe disorder of galactose metabolism (Benign Galactosemia).
**UDP-hexose-4-epimerase (Option C):** isomerises UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose. Its deficiency leads to a less severe disorder of galactose metabolism.
**Aldolase reductase (Option D):** reduces galactose to galactitol and glucose to sorbitol.
